landing.shot.title: One Film, Four Shots
landing.shot.subtitle: Every zombie love story that broke the internet follows the same shot list:
landing.shot.s1.title: The Cabin
landing.shot.s1.desc: A tight close-up on a tearful face: the survivor trembles in the dark cabin with the handgun still lowered at their side, unable to raise it, while the zombified loved one walks closer through the dust.
landing.shot.s2.title: The Undead Face
landing.shot.s2.desc: An extreme close-up: pale grey skin, cloudy eyes, dark veins — frightening, yet still unmistakably the person you recognised in photo two.
landing.shot.s3.title: The Choice
landing.shot.s3.desc: The gun falls from the survivor's hands and both arms open in invitation. The zombie crosses the last few metres, stumbles in, and rests its head against their shoulder.
landing.shot.s4.title: The Match Cut
landing.shot.s4.desc: At the moment of contact, the cabin becomes a golden wheat field at sunset. The same embrace continues unbroken across the cut, both of them alive again.

landing.how.photos.title: How to pick the two photos
landing.how.photos.p1: Same two people in both frames. Photo one hands the model the survivor, photo two the one who has turned — two unrelated images leave it with nobody to carry across the four shots.
landing.how.photos.p2: Match the framing. Keep the distance, head height and angle close; a wide shot into a close-up reads as a jump cut.
landing.how.photos.p3: Light both photos alike. The film already plans its own turn from cold cabin light to golden sunset, so matching your two inputs keeps the faces continuous instead of forcing a relight on top of them.
landing.how.photos.p4: Give each photo its role. Photo one is the survivor — the face that cannot raise the gun; photo two is the one who has turned, the face the extreme close-up finds.
landing.how.photos.p5: Order is casting. Photo one becomes the survivor, photo two the undead — swap them and the gun is held by the wrong face.

landing.faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
landing.faq.q1: What is the AI zombie trend?
landing.faq.a1: A viral format where two photos become a 15-second mini film: one of you has already turned, the other holds a gun they cannot bring themselves to fire, and the closing distance hard-cuts into an embrace in a golden wheat field — cinematic, scored to a trending song. It has blown up across TikTok, and you can now make your own from any two photos.
landing.faq.q2: How many photos do I need?
landing.faq.a2: Exactly two. Front-facing, well-lit faces give the most recognizable result.
landing.faq.q3: How long does a render take?
landing.faq.a3: Usually 10–15 minutes. The film keeps rendering even if you close the tab — it waits in your library.
landing.faq.a4: Credits are refunded to your balance automatically. You never pay for a film you did not get.
landing.faq.a5: Yes. Your browser re-encodes each photo before it is uploaded, which discards EXIF data such as GPS coordinates — the location never leaves your device. Photos are used only for that render, and every photo you stage with us is deleted from storage within 24 hours, whether the render succeeded or failed. They are never used to train models.
landing.faq.a6: No. One-time credit packs, as low as {price} per film — buy once, use whenever the trend comes back around.
landing.faq.q7: How is this different from a general video model?
landing.faq.a7: A general model has no ceiling, but the prompt, the edit, the soundtrack and the per-platform export are all yours — hours on the first try. Here the scene templates are already tuned on the server: two photos, one story, a film in 10–15 minutes. For a 40-second multi-scene piece, the general-model route suits you better.
landing.faq.a8: A template site gives you a zombie look on one photo — fast, with almost no decisions. This trend is a four-shot film carried by two identities: how the survivor and the one they love are held through the cabin and the wheat field. The grade and the soundtrack are done in one pass here, and the people, outfits and pacing belong to your film alone.
landing.faq.q9: Can I turn anyone's photo into a zombie?
landing.faq.a9: No. Before a render is accepted the generator makes you declare that the faces are your own, your own pet, or people who agreed to appear — no children, no celebrities or public figures — and that declaration is stored with the job. The prompt, the photos and the finished clip are each screened, and nothing is published publicly unless you opted in at submit time. If a clip used your likeness without permission, email jiusongvip@gmail.com and we take it down.
landing.faq.q10: What is the difference between 480p and 720p?
landing.faq.a10: Both tiers render the same 15-second, four-shot film from your two photos, with the same grade and soundtrack. 480p is the size the trend is normally posted at, and on a phone its grain and shadow read as part of the look. 720p resolves faces, hair and the wheat-field light more cleanly, which is what you want for a projector, a printed frame or a YouTube upload. Packs are plain credits, so one balance covers both tiers.
landing.faq.q11: Who is behind AI Zombie Trend?
landing.faq.a11: An independent project, not a big-media studio. The developer maintains the generator and the example-wall sharing policy, and answers support mail at jiusongvip@gmail.com — the About page has the full story.

landing.spec.title: What you upload and what you get
landing.spec.intro: Four things define the transaction: two photographs going in, one 15-second film coming out, one-time credits as payment, and a private library as the delivery channel. Every number below is the product as it is built, not as it is marketed.
landing.spec.c1.title: Input · two photos
landing.spec.c1.b1: Photo one is the survivor — the face that stays human and holds the gun.
landing.spec.c1.b2: Photo two becomes the zombie: a partner, a best friend, a parent, or a dog or cat.
landing.spec.c1.b3: JPG, PNG or WebP, up to 10 MB each, one face close to the camera.
landing.spec.c1.b4: Your browser re-encodes both pictures before upload, so EXIF data such as GPS never leaves the device.
landing.spec.c2.title: Output · one 15-second film
landing.spec.c2.b1: Four locked shots: the cabin at 0–4 seconds, the undead close-up at 4–6, the choice at 6–10, the memory at 10–15.
landing.spec.c2.b2: 9:16 for Reels and TikTok, or 16:9 for YouTube and a widescreen story.
landing.spec.c2.b3: 480p for 20 credits, 720p for 40 — the same film, resolved faces and hair.
landing.spec.c2.b4: Scene audio is written into the brief and arrives with the picture. Neither tier carries a watermark.
landing.spec.c3.title: Payment · one-time credits
landing.spec.c3.b1: One film for $5.99, or $2.10 per film on the 60-film pack.
landing.spec.c3.b2: 20 credits per standard film, 40 per HD film, deducted once when the job is accepted.
landing.spec.c3.b3: Credits never expire, and there is no subscription to cancel.
landing.spec.c3.b4: A render that fails returns its credits to your balance automatically.
landing.spec.c4.title: Delivery · your private library
landing.spec.c4.b1: Every finished film lands in My Videos with its own private link, readable from any device you sign in on.
landing.spec.c4.b2: Usually ready in 10–15 minutes. The queue keeps working after you close the tab.
landing.spec.c4.b3: Download the finished MP4 at full quality and post it wherever you like.
landing.spec.c4.b4: Nothing reaches the public example wall unless you tick that box at submit time.
landing.modes.title: Four stories, one grammar
landing.modes.intro: The cabin, the lowered gun and the wheat field stay identical across all four modes. What changes is who is standing in the doorway: the template rewrites the relationship line, the pronouns, and the way Character B crosses the room around it.
landing.modes.couple.title: The couple film
landing.modes.couple.body: You are the survivor; your partner is the one who has already turned. This is the mode the trend was born in, and the one that leans hardest on the recognition beat — the moment Character B stops mid-step because something familiar flickers through the cloudy eyes. Two headshots of a couple you actually photograph together give the model the most to preserve.
landing.modes.couple.tip: Best when both faces are roughly the same distance from the camera, so neither character is rebuilt at a different scale.
landing.modes.pet.title: The pet film
landing.modes.pet.body: The owner holds the gun; the dog or cat in photo two is the undead animal. The breed, coat and size in your reference are held across the whole clip, and the animal keeps its own way of moving — dragging itself closer with a stiff gait rather than walking upright. Its undead read is grey fur, cloudy eyes and dark veins, frightening but unmistakably still your pet.
landing.modes.pet.tip: A clear side-on photo of the animal, with the whole body in frame, keeps the breed and proportions honest.
landing.modes.friend.title: The best-friend film
landing.modes.friend.body: Two people who are not a couple: the survivor and the friend who showed up anyway. The same four shots carry a different charge here, because the arms opened at 6 seconds read as loyalty rather than romance. Nothing about the storyboard changes — only the relationship the opening line declares.
landing.modes.friend.tip: Any two consenting adults work; a group photo is not needed, since each frame supplies one face.
landing.modes.family.title: The family film
landing.modes.family.body: The younger survivor and the elder — a mother or a father — who has turned. Photo two is read as the parent: Character B is the older of the two references, and the embrace at the end of the cabin scene lands as a child holding a parent one last time. This is the mode people submit when the trend touches something personal.
landing.modes.family.tip: Choose photos where both faces are legible; a parent photographed from behind gives the model less identity to carry.
landing.photos.title: Which photos make the best film
landing.photos.intro: Two ordinary photographs are the entire input, so the quality of the film is decided before you press generate. Five things matter, in this order.
landing.photos.s1.title: One face, close to the camera
landing.photos.s1.body: Both identities are held across fifteen seconds and four lighting setups, which the model does by reading the reference in detail. A face that fills a good share of the frame, in even light, with eyes open and nothing over the brow, gives it something to preserve. Sun-bleached selfies, heavy shadow, motion blur and sunglasses all cost recognisability.
landing.photos.s2.title: One subject per picture
landing.photos.s2.body: Each upload supplies one character. A group photo forces the model to choose a face from it, and the two characters end up related to each other in ways you did not pick. Crop to the person or the animal that should star.
landing.photos.s3.title: Match the two photographs
landing.photos.s3.body: A studio portrait next to a beach selfie gives two different camera distances, colour casts and head sizes to reconcile. You do not need matching outfits — the film dresses both characters in clean everyday clothing — but similar framing and lighting make the finished clip read as one scene rather than two composites.
landing.photos.s4.title: Upload order is the story
landing.photos.s4.body: Photo one is always the survivor. Photo two is always the one who has turned. Swap them and you swap who lowers the gun and who is held in the memory at the end, so check the two labelled frames before submitting.
landing.photos.s5.title: Faces you are allowed to use
landing.photos.s5.body: Your own face, your own pet, and other adults who have agreed to appear. Not children, and not celebrities or public figures — the generator asks you to declare that before it accepts a job, and the declaration is kept with the render.
landing.format.title: Choose 9:16 for Reels or 16:9 for a wider story
landing.format.intro: The story is fixed at fifteen seconds and four shots; the frame is yours to pick, and the two options behave differently on the same storyboard.
landing.format.v.title: 9:16 — the size the trend travels at
landing.format.v.body: Reels, TikTok and Shorts are vertical, and this is the ratio the format was cut for. It keeps the survivor tight in the cabin, holds the undead close-up at shot two uncomfortable, and lets the camera pull back up through the wheat at the end. If the film is going straight onto a phone feed, start here.
landing.format.w.title: 16:9 — for YouTube, a projector, or a wider embrace
landing.format.w.body: Landscape spends the same fifteen seconds on geography. The cabin reads as an abandoned room rather than a dark portrait, and the final pull-back shows how much empty golden field the two of them are standing in, which is the emotional payoff of the fourth shot. Choose it for YouTube uploads, an embedded copy on your own site, or a frame you intend to print.
landing.format.n.title: What never changes between the two
landing.format.n.body: Duration, shot order, colour grade, scene audio and resolution tier are identical in both ratios. Nothing is cropped off the storyboard when you go horizontal — the same four beats, composed for a wider frame.
landing.tier.title: 480p or 720p — what the extra credits buy
landing.tier.intro: Resolution is the only thing that costs more here. The story, the grade and the sound are the same brief, and each tier is its own endpoint on the render farm.
landing.tier.s.title: 480p · 20 credits per film
landing.tier.s.body: The size the trend is normally posted at. On a phone screen at Reels scale, the grain and the deep shadow of the cabin read as part of the look, and the file is the lightest to upload back to a social app. This is the tier every pack is priced against.
landing.tier.h.title: 720p · 40 credits per film
landing.tier.h.body: Twice the pixels land where the film needs them: facial detail during the tears of shot one, the veins and cloudy eyes of shot two, individual hair in the backlight, and the wheat itself in the last five seconds. Pick it for YouTube, a projector, a printed frame, or any copy you want to survive being re-uploaded.
landing.tier.m.title: How the math works on each pack
landing.tier.m.body: Packs are plain credits, so one balance covers both tiers. A Trio Pack holds 60 credits: three standard films or one HD film with credits left over for a third of the next. A Ten Pack holds 200: ten standard or five HD. The 60-film pack holds 1,200: sixty standard or thirty HD. Because HD costs 40, the film count printed on a pack always describes the standard tier.
landing.tier.c.title: What both tiers already include
landing.tier.c.body: No watermark, no credit stamp, no reduced duration and no silent export on either tier. The difference you are paying for is resolution, nothing else.
landing.cut.title: Why the embrace cuts to a golden field
landing.cut.body1: The fourth shot is a match cut. The embrace begins in the dark cabin and continues, without a break in the movement, into the same two bodies standing in a wheat field at sunset. Because the composition and the gesture carry across the join, the cut reads as one action rather than two separate clips, which is what makes the reversal feel like memory instead of a transition effect.
landing.cut.q: In film, a match cut is a cut from one shot to another in which the composition of the two shots are matched by the action or subject and subject matter.
landing.cut.body2: The same device is why the grade splits in two. The first ten seconds are desaturated and cold, lit through dirty cabin windows; the last five are golden, backlit and warm. Editors describe that pairing as the payoff of a well-motivated match cut.
landing.cut.adobe: Adobe’s guide to match cuts in film
landing.cut.h3: What the model has to hold across the cut
landing.cut.h3body: Both faces, both hairstyles and both body proportions have to survive the join; the embrace has to be continuous on either side of it; and the clothing and light switch to the other camp instantly. The last five seconds only read as memory while all three hold at once. Loose any one of them and what the audience sees is a special effect.
landing.deliver.title: Queue, consent, and what we delete
landing.deliver.intro: Nothing about a generation is hidden from you: how long it takes, what is checked before it runs, what you have to declare, and what happens to your photographs afterwards.
landing.deliver.s1.title: While your film renders
landing.deliver.s1.body: The job enters a queue and the credits are reserved at that moment. Most films finish in 10–15 minutes, and the queue does not care whether your tab stays open — come back to My Videos and the finished film is waiting with its own private link.
landing.deliver.s2.title: What gets screened, in order
landing.deliver.s2.body: Three checks run in sequence: the story text, then each uploaded photograph, then the finished clip. They happen in that order for a reason — the cheap ones come first, so a submission that cannot proceed is stopped before any credits are committed. A render blocked by a check is not charged.
landing.deliver.s3.title: The declaration you make
landing.deliver.s3.body: Before the render is accepted, you tick that the faces are your own, your own pet, or adults who agreed to appear. No children, no public figures. That declaration is stored with the job, which is what lets us act on a report instead of guessing. If a clip used your likeness without permission, write to jiusongvip@gmail.com and it comes down.
landing.deliver.s4.title: What we delete
landing.deliver.s4.body: The photographs you stage are removed from storage within 24 hours whether the render succeeded or failed, and they are never used to train models. EXIF is stripped in your browser before upload, so location data never reaches us at all. The finished film is yours: it stays in your private library, and the public example wall only ever shows a clip whose owner opted in.
landing.deliver.s5.title: If it does not come out right
landing.deliver.s5.body: A failed render refunds its credits automatically — you never pay for a film you did not get. Re-submit with clearer photographs rather than a different story: in practice the input images are where a weak result starts. Refunds of money already paid follow the Refund Policy.

landing.faq.q12: Does the order I upload the two photos matter?
landing.faq.a12: Yes, and it is the single most common reason a film is not what someone expected. Photo one is always the survivor — the one who lowers the gun and opens their arms. Photo two is always the one who has turned. Swap them and you swap who is human in the memory at the end.
landing.faq.q13: Can I make the video with my dog or cat?
landing.faq.a13: That is one of the four story modes. Put your own face in photo one and the animal in photo two: the breed, coat and size in the reference are held through the clip, and the undead animal crosses the room its own way — dragging itself closer with a stiff gait rather than walking. A full-body side-on photo works best.
landing.faq.q14: Is there a version for a parent?
landing.faq.a14: Yes, the family mode. Photo one is the younger survivor and photo two is read as the parent, the elder of the two references, so the embrace at the end of the cabin scene lands as a child holding a mother or father. People tend to pick this mode when the trend touches something personal rather than playful.
landing.faq.q15: Does the film come with audio?
landing.faq.a15: Sound is written into the brief rather than added afterwards: cabin ambience, faint wind, shaky breathing and sobbing in the first ten seconds, an unsettling low rumble over the undead close-up, and a soft swell as the embrace becomes the memory. That is generated scene audio, not a licensed track — which keeps every frame you download free of anyone else’s copyright, and leaves the trending sound to you at post time.
landing.faq.q16: Will the two people look exactly like my photos?
landing.faq.a16: Both identities are held across all fifteen seconds and both lighting setups — face, recognisable hairstyle and body proportions are part of the brief, and the memory restores Character B to the appearance in the reference. It is a generation, not a photocopy: expression, clothing and camera angle are the model’s, so a second take of the same two photos is a different film. Clear, front-lit references are what move the result closer to the people you know.
landing.faq.q17: Can I post the film on TikTok or Reels?
landing.faq.a17: Yes. Downloads carry no watermark, and 9:16 is cut for exactly that use. Add your own music in the app you post from if you want a trending sound under it — the file arrives with scene audio, which is easy to replace and impossible to license for you.
landing.pgp.how.title: How credits work
landing.pgp.how.body: A credit pack is a balance, not a plan. Every render costs a fixed number of credits at the moment the job is accepted — 20 for a 480p film, 40 for 720p — and the balance goes down by that amount and nothing else. There is no per-second billing, no charge for retries you did not submit, and no renewal that happens on its own.
landing.pgp.how.s1.title: What a failed render costs you
landing.pgp.how.s1.body: Nothing. Credits are reserved when the render starts and returned to your balance automatically when the generation fails upstream, when the finished clip is blocked by content review, or when the task is cancelled or expires without producing a film. You can check it yourself: a failed job shows as failed in My Videos, and the credits are back.
landing.pgp.how.s2.title: What never runs out
landing.pgp.how.s2.body: Credits do not expire and there is no subscription behind a pack. Buy the Ten Pack in October and render your next film the week the trend comes back around. One balance covers both resolution tiers, so you can render a 480p test and a 720p final version out of the same purchase.
landing.pgp.how.s3.title: What you are actually buying
landing.pgp.how.s3.body: One accepted render of the full fifteen-second, four-shot film at the tier you picked, with scene audio, in the aspect ratio you picked, downloadable without a watermark. A second take costs a second set of credits, because it is a second job on the render farm.
landing.pgp.packs.title: Which pack to buy
landing.pgp.packs.intro: The four packs differ only in how many films they fund and what that works out to per film. Here is what each one is actually for.
landing.pgp.packs.single.title: Single Pack — $5.99 for one film
landing.pgp.packs.single.body: The entry point, and the right choice the first time. Twenty credits render one 480p film, so you see what two of your own photographs look like inside the cabin and the wheat field before committing to anything larger. The trend is a format people react to differently, and one film is enough to find out which side you are on.
landing.pgp.packs.trio.title: Trio Pack — $14.99 for three films
landing.pgp.packs.trio.body: Three standard films, or one 720p film with credits still left over. This is the pack for the person who wants a couple version and a pet version and one for a friend, or who knows they will want a second take with different photographs. Per film it costs barely less than the Single Pack; you are buying the option to iterate, not a discount.
landing.pgp.packs.ten.title: Ten Pack — $39.90 for ten films
landing.pgp.packs.ten.body: The pack most people land on once the format has clicked. Ten standard films, or five in 720p, at $3.99 per film. It is enough to run a series — the same two faces across all four story modes, several framing options for different platforms, and room for the retakes that clearer photographs make unnecessary.
landing.pgp.packs.annual.title: Annual Pack — $126.00 for sixty films
landing.pgp.packs.annual.body: Two dollars and ten cents a film, thirty in 720p, and a balance that does not expire. Sized for anyone posting the format regularly: a page that runs the trend weekly, a studio making variations for several couples, or a person who simply expects to make this more than twice.
landing.pgp.compare.title: Cost per film, both tiers
landing.pgp.compare.intro: Same catalog, same credit costs, arithmetic only. Standard means 480p at 20 credits per film, HD means 720p at 40. HD counts are whole films — the remainder stays in your balance.
landing.pgp.compare.note: Per-film cost is pack price divided by whole films at that tier. The Single Pack funds no complete 720p film on its own, which is why that column starts at the Trio.
landing.pgp.included.title: What is already included at every price
landing.pgp.included.intro: Nothing on this list is an upsell, and nothing is gated behind a bigger pack.
landing.pgp.included.b1: The complete fifteen-second film — all four shots, the grade split and the match cut, in both tiers.
landing.pgp.included.b2: All four story modes: couple, pet, best friend and family. Picking a mode never changes the price.
landing.pgp.included.b3: 9:16 and 16:9 framing at the same cost, and scene audio generated with the picture.
landing.pgp.included.b4: Watermark-free downloads in MP4, yours to post anywhere.
landing.pgp.included.b5: Automatic credit return on any render that does not deliver a film.
landing.pgp.included.b6: A private library with a link per film, readable from every device you sign in on.
landing.pgp.refund.title: Money back, and where it applies
landing.pgp.refund.body: Two separate mechanisms, and it is worth keeping them apart. A render that does not produce a film refunds its credits automatically, with no email and no request. Cash refunds cover the purchase itself: an unused pack where none of its credits have been spent, claimed within 7 days, comes back in full to the card or account you paid with, and a purchase that never reached your balance is refunded in full once confirmed. Approved refunds are issued within 5 business days. The Refund Policy states both rules in full.
landing.pgp.faq.title: Pricing questions
landing.pgp.faq.q1: Why does 720p cost twice the credits?
landing.pgp.faq.a1: The two tiers are separate endpoints on the render farm and the HD one is billed at a higher rate per second of generated video. The film, the story and the audio are identical — you are paying for resolution and nothing else, which is why 480p is the default.
landing.pgp.faq.q2: Can I combine credits from different packs?
landing.pgp.faq.a2: Yes. Packs add to one balance rather than sitting in separate buckets, so a Single Pack and a Ten Pack are spent interchangeably. The balance is what the generate button checks.
landing.pgp.faq.q3: Is there a cheaper way to test before I commit?
landing.pgp.faq.a3: The example wall on this site and on /examples shows films made here from two photographs, with the story each one tells. Read a frame or two before buying: the format is unmistakable once you have seen it, and the only thing a test render can tell you is how your own faces sit inside it.
landing.pgp.faq.q4: Do prices change with the story mode or the aspect ratio?
landing.pgp.faq.a4: No. Every mode and both framings cost the same 20 or 40 credits, because the render is the same job with a different opening line and a different canvas.
landing.pgp.faq.q5: What happens if I run out of credits halfway through an idea?
landing.pgp.faq.a5: Nothing is lost — each film is one complete job, so there is no half-finished purchase to top up. Buy another pack whenever you want the next take; the earlier balance is still there, since credits do not expire.
landing.exg.look.title: What to look for in each clip
landing.exg.look.intro: Three things decide whether a zombie film lands, and every example on this wall is built to be checked against them.
landing.exg.look.s1.title: The two faces stay the same people
landing.exg.look.s1.body: One film is four shots across two completely different lighting setups, and the two characters are supplied as nothing but photographs. Watch a face from the cold cabin interior into the golden field at the end: hairstyle, proportions and the shape of the eyes are what tell you whether the model held the person or invented a lookalike. That continuity is the whole reason both photos go in as character references instead of a single starting frame.
landing.exg.look.s2.title: The embrace carries across the cut
landing.exg.look.s2.body: Shot three ends with arms opening in the cabin; shot four begins with the same bodies already closing in the wheat field. In a good result the movement has no seam — the hug continues through the cut rather than restarting on the other side of it. That single join is the technique the whole format rests on, and it is worth pausing a clip at exactly that frame.
landing.exg.look.s3.title: The colour tells you which half you are in
landing.exg.look.s3.body: The first ten seconds are desaturated and blue-grey, lit through dirty cabin windows with dust in the light. The last five are golden and backlit, with movement in the wheat. The contrast is the emotional argument of the piece: cold and frightening on one side, warm and lost on the other. A clip where both halves look the same grade has lost the point of the format.
landing.exg.made.title: How these films were made
landing.exg.made.body: Each one is a single request: two photographs, one story mode, one resolution tier. The scene brief, the shot order, the timings, the grade and the sound design are all fixed on our side and never exposed as a prompt box, so there is no tuning step between an example here and what your own two photographs become. Where a card lists a model name, that is the endpoint the film ran through — 480p and 720p are separate endpoints at the same picture.
landing.exg.made.label: Every film on this wall is AI-generated fiction, marked as such on the card. The faces are characters rendered from photographs supplied by the people in them or with their agreement, and nothing here depicts a real event.
landing.exg.modes.title: The same four shots, four relationships
landing.exg.modes.intro: Filter the wall by story and the storyboard stays identical while the cast changes. That is the useful thing to study: what a dog moves like compared with a person, and what the same embrace reads like when the two people are friends rather than lovers.
landing.exg.modes.couple: Couple — the original form of the trend: the gun, the hesitation, and the partner who came back to the door anyway.
landing.exg.modes.pet: Pet — the owner opens both arms and the animal drags itself across the room to rest its head on their shoulder, which is what makes these clips land hardest.
landing.exg.modes.friend: Friend — two people who showed up for each other, with the same beats read as loyalty instead of romance.
landing.exg.modes.family: Family — the younger survivor and the parent who has turned, ending on a child holding an adult one last time.
landing.exg.next.title: From an example to your own film
landing.exg.next.body: Pick the card whose story is closest to yours and open the workbench from it: the mode comes preselected, and the only decision left is which two photographs. Everything else on this page — the shot order, the grade, the timings — is already handled by the same template that made the clip you are looking at.
landing.exg.faq.title: Questions about the examples
landing.exg.faq.q1: Are these made with real users’ photos?
landing.exg.faq.a1: Only with the owner’s agreement. The example wall is opt-in at submit time and off by default, so a film appears here only if the person who rendered it chose to share it. Every card carries the AI-generated mark, and a clip that should not be on the wall can be reported straight from it — accidentally shared examples come down.
landing.exg.faq.q2: Will my film look exactly like the example I clicked?
landing.exg.faq.a2: It will follow the same storyboard: the same four shots, the same cut, the same grade split and sound design. What differs is the cast — your faces, your hair, your animal — and the model’s own variation, which is why two takes of one pair of photographs are two different films.
landing.exg.faq.q3: Why do some cards show a model name?
landing.exg.faq.a3: The wall spans films made on more than one endpoint, including the 480p and 720p tiers and the earlier single-shot examples. The label tells you which one produced that picture; the story template behind it is the same.
landing.exg.faq.q4: Can I use an example as my own starting point?
landing.exg.faq.a4: Yes — every card links into the workbench with its story mode already selected, so you are starting from the same brief with your own two photographs in the slots.
blog.h1: Guides to the AI zombie trend
blog.intro: Everything we know about the format, written down: what the trend is and where it came from, how a two-photo zombie film is actually made, and what happens to a face once someone uploads it. These are the pages we point people to before they spend anything — a fifteen-second film is easy to make, but it is worth knowing what you are looking at first.

blog.written.title: How these guides are written
blog.written.body: By the same person who maintains the generator, from the product as it is actually built: shot timings come from the story template, prices from the billing catalog, upload limits from the frame slots, deletion windows from the privacy policy. When any of those numbers change, the affected guide is updated and the date on it moves with the change. Where a guide borrows a definition rather than writing one, the source is named and linked instead of paraphrased.
